device: Chorale as a fixed line (cantus firmus)
content: A chorale tune in long notes is one layer. The other voices have their own material around it
parameters: Bach, movement 1: chorale in G major above a chorus in E minor
example: St Matthew Passion, movements 1 and 29

content: A line imitates itself at a fixed distance in time and pitch, while a chorale tune goes through the texture
parameters: Five variations in canon
example: Bach, Canonic Variations on "Vom Himmel hoch", BWV 769

device: Canon that goes up by step
content: The canon ends one whole tone higher than it started. Each repeat is one tone higher
parameters: Six repeats bring the canon back to the first key, one octave higher
example: Bach, The Musical Offering, the canon "per tonos"

content: Voices enter one after the other with the same subject. In a stretto "the answer enters before the subject is completed"
example: St Matthew Passion, "Laß ihn kreuzigen"

content: A short bass line repeats. The upper voices change above it
parameters: The form is usually serious and in triple metre
example: Bach, Crucifixus of the Mass in B minor; Purcell, Dido's lament

content: A bass that goes down a fourth from the key note to the fifth note. In the chromatic form each step is a semitone
parameters: Crucifixus (measured): 21 percent of the bass moves are semitones, 70 percent are repeated notes
example: Crucifixus; the bass of "Erbarme dich" goes down from B to E by scale steps

content: A line that fills a fourth with semitones. The name means a hard passage
example: The bass of "Buß und Reu": F-sharp, E-sharp, E, D, C-sharp

content: The bass stays on one note while the harmony moves above it
parameters: Longest pedal notes of the corpus (measured): 48 quarter notes (St John Passion, movement 1), 13 ("O Mensch, bewein"), 9 ("Wir setzen uns")
example: The first bars of the opening choruses of the two Passions

content: Two choirs answer each other with short calls and questions
example: St Matthew Passion, movement 1 ("Sehet!" - "Wen?")

device: Solo instrument as a second voice
content: In an aria, the instrument and the voice have the same material and answer each other
parameters: Violin: 2.2 notes for each quarter note; alto: 0.9 (measured)
example: "Erbarme dich"

content: Long soft chords of the strings around the words of one person
example: The words of Jesus in the St Matthew Passion

content: A figure of the instruments shows one word of the text: drops, blows, trembling
example: Flutes in "Buß und Reu"; strings in "Erbarm es Gott"; bass in "O Schmerz"

content: One voice moves by step. A second voice has only the notes of one triad. "The melody and the accompaniment is one"
parameters: The triad voice takes the nearest note of the triad above or below the melody note
example: Pärt, Für Alina; Passio

content: The note values come from the words. A syllable is short, medium, or long: the punctuation and the position in the phrase decide
parameters: Last word before a full stop: each syllable long. Stressed syllable of the last word before a comma: medium. All other syllables: short
example: Pärt, Passio

device: A pitch centre for each person
content: Each person of the story has a note value and a pitch centre. Christ has the longest and lowest notes
parameters: Fifths in a chain: D, A, E, B. The centre of Christ is E
example: Pärt, Passio

content: All voices have the same line, but each voice has its own note value (a prolation canon or mensuration canon)
parameters: A canon "by augmentation" has the note values doubled
example: Pärt, Cantus in Memoriam Benjamin Britten (a canon on one motif in A minor)

content: All voices sing the same chorale phrase, each in its own tempo. They wait at the end of the phrase until all are there
parameters: Three phrases of a chorale of Bach; soft start and soft end
example: Nystedt, Immortal Bach

content: Two players have the same short figure. One goes a little faster: the figure moves against itself and comes back to the unison
parameters: First an echo, then each note two times, then a complex ring
example: Reich; in Richter's version of Vivaldi the old figures are in loops and in phase shifts

content: Take a small part of an old work. Repeat it and change its context. Remove the rest
parameters: Richter removed 75 percent of the material of Vivaldi
example: Richter, Recomposed: The Four Seasons

content: Each variation removes one note from the start and one from the end of the theme. Later the theme comes back note by note, backwards
parameters: The theme of The Musical Offering; the full theme comes only at the end
example: Gubaidulina, Offertorium

content: One line goes from instrument to instrument. The change of colour shows the motifs of the line
parameters: Gubaidulina gives the theme of Bach to different instruments, as Webern did
example: Webern, Ricercata; Gubaidulina, Offertorium

content: Many voices play canons at small distances and different speeds. The ear hears a texture, not the lines
parameters: Ligeti: "you cannot actually hear the polyphony, the canon"
example: Ligeti, Atmosphères and Lontano

device: Two styles at the same time
content: Old tonal music and new music sound together or one after the other
example: Pärt, Credo; Schnittke, Concerto Grosso No. 1

device: The chorale in a foreign language
content: A chorale of Bach comes into music with a different harmony. The plain chords are an event
parameters: Berg: the row has triads, and the last section is a set of chorale variations. Penderecki: a major triad comes only two times
example: Berg, Violin Concerto; Penderecki, St Luke Passion

device: The old form with new content
content: Keep the form of a Passion of Bach (story, response, chorale) and put a different story or a different musical language into it
parameters: Lang: 15 numbers; story numbers and response numbers in turn; the titles of the response numbers come from the text of Picander
example: Lang, the little match girl passion; Kagel, Sankt-Bach-Passion

content: The music has the harmony of the old piece from the start, but not its form. The quotation comes late and is short
parameters: Shaw: "modular sequences strung together out of context"; the chorale can be recognised at about the middle
example: Shaw, Punctum

device: One melody shared by two players (hocket)
content: Two voices have the notes of one melody in turns: one sounds while the other rests
example: Medieval music; used again in the 20th century

device: One line in more than one form (heterophony)
content: Players have the same melody at the same time, each with a different rhythm or with ornaments
example: Usual in many traditions outside Europe

device: Rhythm cycle and pitch cycle of different lengths
content: A rhythm pattern repeats in one voice. The pitches repeat in a cycle of a different length (isorhythm)
parameters: The pattern of the rhythm is the talea; the pattern of the pitches is the color
example: Motets of the 14th century; used again in the 20th century

content: A sound seems to go down for ever: when a line goes out at the bottom, the same line comes in at the top
parameters: A sound of sine waves at octaves
example: The Shepard scale; the same idea is possible with the entries of a canon
